title: Snowball Earth and Hothouse Earth
objective: After this level you can describe Earth's most extreme past climates and what the rocks tell us about them.
summary: Rocks suggest ice once reached the Equator, until volcanic carbon dioxide thawed the planet and left cap carbonates behind. At the other extreme, ice-free poles grew Arctic palms.

cards.headline: Earth has frozen near the Equator, and grown palm trees in the Arctic.
cards.body: Both extremes left clues in the rocks. Read them, and the same control knob keeps showing up.

cards.headline: Snowball Earth
cards.body: The Cryogenian Period, about 720 to 635 million years ago, takes its name from the Greek for frost or ice, and for good reason: much if not all of Earth froze. The key clue is ice-laid deposits that, magnetic evidence shows, formed near the Equator. If ice reached the tropics, the Snowball Earth hypothesis says, it reached from pole to pole. Some scientists argue for a 'Slushball' with open water; the debate isn't settled.

cards.headline: How to thaw a snowball
cards.body: Volcanoes never stopped venting carbon dioxide. Weathering and photosynthesis, which normally pull it back out, were suppressed on a frozen planet. So the gas built up until its greenhouse warming melted the ice. The rocks record the flip: layered limestone or dolomite, called cap carbonates, sits directly on the glacial deposits at over 50 places, from Death Valley to Namibia.

cards.headline: Hothouse Earth
cards.body: Now the other extreme. About 56 million years ago, the poles had no ice caps, and palm trees grew above the Arctic Circle. A 2024 study that rebuilt 485 million years of global temperature summed up the pattern. In paleoclimatologist Jessica Tierney's words: 'carbon dioxide is the dominant control on global temperatures across geological time.'

questions.prompt: What were the poles like about 56 million years ago, in a hothouse Earth?

options.label: Buried under ice sheets reaching the tropics
Much as they are today, with thick ice caps
options.rationale: The poles had no ice caps then.

options.label: Free of ice caps, with palm trees above the Arctic Circle
Covered by shallow seas full of cap carbonates
options.rationale: Cap carbonates mark the end of a snowball.

questions.explanation: About 56 million years ago the poles were free of ice caps, and palm trees lived above the Arctic Circle.

questions.prompt: Why did Snowball Earth eventually thaw?

options.label: The Sun grew much brighter within a few years
options.rationale: The level credits carbon dioxide from volcanoes.

options.label: Cap carbonates absorbed sunlight and warmed the ice
options.rationale: Cap carbonates formed after the thaw.

options.label: Ice sheets slid off the continents into the sea
options.rationale: The ice melted as greenhouse warming built up.

options.label: Volcanic carbon dioxide built up with little removing it

questions.explanation: With weathering and photosynthesis suppressed, volcanic carbon dioxide accumulated until its greenhouse warming melted the ice.

questions.prompt: Some cap carbonates are limestone. Using Level 6, what is limestone mostly made of?

options.label: Quartz grains held together by cement

questions.explanation: Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate, usually the mineral calcite, often from the shells of sea life.
